meta.subtitle: Leading global alternative asset manager with over $1 trillion of AUM; a measured BUY with shares near the 52-week low

analystCommentary: We rate Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. (BAM) a BUY with a $50 to $60 target range. BAM is a leading global alternative asset manager across infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate, and credit, and it earns fee-based revenue on the capital it manages for institutional and private-wealth clients. FY25 revenue rose {+ +16.7% +} to $3.9B and net income reached $2.4B. The trailing net margin is 74.8%, reflecting an asset-light, fee-driven model. The shares trade at $46.01, near the low end of a $42.20 to $62.57 52-week range, at 26.6x trailing earnings and 17.9x sales. The street reads Buy on consensus with a $57.52 target, but it is split almost evenly at 9 Buy, 8 Hold and 1 Sell. Our probability-weighted fair value is about $52, an expected upside near +12.9% from the current price, against a bear case about 17.4% below it. A reward/risk of roughly 0.74x keeps this a measured BUY rather than a high-conviction one.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. describes itself as a leading global alternative asset manager, headquartered in New York, with over $1 trillion of Assets Under Management across infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate, and credit. It offers alternative investment products to over 2,500 institutional clients and, in total, approximately 69,000 clients, and it earns asset management income for doing so. The company runs 59 unique active strategies and draws on over 5,800 investment and asset management professionals and employees across 32 global offices, with a dedicated team of roughly 150 focused on the private wealth channel. Its products fall into long-term private funds, permanent capital vehicles and perpetual strategies, and liquid strategies, invested across five principal platforms in infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate, and credit. The Class A Shares are co-listed on the NYSE and the TSX under the symbol BAM, and the company operates as a subsidiary of Brookfield Corporation. Management evaluates performance using non-GAAP measures it defines itself, including Fee-Bearing Capital, Fee Revenues, Fee-Related Earnings and Distributable Earnings.

thesis.body: The investment case rests on scale and fee-bearing capital. BAM reported FY25 revenue of $3.9B, up {+ +16.7% +}, with net income of $2.4B. Capital expenditure is negligible, so free cash flow of $2.1B in FY25 tracked operating cash flow, and the trailing net margin reflects the asset-light nature of a fee manager. Consensus expects FY26E revenue of about $6.1B, a step-up the market is pricing at 26.6x trailing earnings and 17.9x sales. The counter-case is that those multiples leave little room for error: the shares sit near their 52-week low of $42.20, and the FY26E step-up consensus expects is large relative to recent quarterly trends. At $46.01 the risk and reward are positive but not commanding, which supports a measured BUY.

catalysts: Consensus sees EPS rising across FY26E and FY27E; delivery against that estimate path would support the multiple.
Continued growth in Fee-Bearing Capital across the five investment platforms would lift fee revenue.
A re-rating back toward the consensus analyst target would recover much of the recent share-price decline.
An easing of monetary policy, after the Federal Reserve's rate cuts in late 2025, would aid fundraising and asset values.
risks: Valuation is full and the shares already sit near their 52-week low; a de-rating toward the low end of the analyst target range would erase the upside.
The FY25 dividend has run ahead of both earnings and free cash flow, and total equity has slipped three years running.
Part of BAM's reported results sits outside management's internal-control evaluation following the 2025 Arrangement, per the 10-K.
The analyst panel is split almost evenly between Buy and Hold, a divergence that signals low conviction on how the year plays out.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue grew from $3.1B in FY23 to $3.4B in FY24 ({+ +7.6% +}) and $3.9B in FY25 ({+ +16.7% +}), so growth accelerated in the most recent year. Net income was $2.1B in both FY23 and FY24 and rose to $2.4B in FY25; diluted EPS climbed from $1.16 to $1.34 to $1.52 over the same span. As an asset manager, BAM reports no gross-margin, operating-income or EBITDA line, so margin analysis runs through net income: the trailing net margin is 74.8%, consistent with an asset-light fee model. In the latest quarter, Q2'26 ended June 30, 2026, revenue was about $1B and rose {+ +12.5% +} year over year; the snapshot rounds that growth to 12%. There is no operating-income line, so the quarter's operating margin is not meaningful. The company frames its own performance through non-GAAP measures, namely Fee-Bearing Capital, Fee Revenues, Fee-Related Earnings and Distributable Earnings, whose values the pack does not provide beyond Fee-Bearing Capital by platform. Consensus looks for FY26E revenue of about $6.1B and EPS of $1.83, then FY27E revenue of $7.1B and EPS of $2.17.
financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet the pack shows is light on detail. Cash and short-term investments rose from $0.0B in FY23 to $0.4B in FY24 and $1.6B in FY25. Total equity edged down over the three years, from $9.3B in FY23 to $9.1B in FY24 and $8.9B in FY25. The pack does not disclose total debt, net debt or a current ratio, so leverage and liquidity coverage cannot be assessed from it; net-debt/EBITDA and interest coverage are shown as not available. The combination of declining equity and a rising cash balance is consistent with a distribution that has outrun earnings, which is taken up under cash flow.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow rose steadily from $1.4B in FY23 to $1.6B in FY24 and $2.1B in FY25. Capital expenditure is negligible, about -$9M in FY25, so free cash flow matched operating cash flow in each year, and the FCF margin expanded from 45.3% to 47.4% to 53.0%. The trailing FCF yield is 3.2%. The pressure point is the payout: dividends paid grew to $2.5B in FY24 and $2.8B in FY25, and the FY25 distribution outran both net income of $2.4B and free cash flow. Cash still rose rather than fell over the period, which implies the shortfall was funded outside these lines; the pack does not detail financing flows. A payout that runs ahead of free cash flow is sustainable only while other sources fill the gap, so coverage of the distribution is the item to watch.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: BAM trades at 26.6x trailing earnings and 17.9x sales, with a forward P/E of 25.1x on next-twelve-month estimates and about 21.2x on FY27E earnings. EV/EBITDA is not available because the company reports no EBITDA line. These are full multiples: the price-to-sales figure in particular reflects the asset-light, high-margin fee model, where a high net margin does much of the work. The peer column is empty in the pack, with peers pending a peer data source, so the multiples stand on their own rather than against a comparable set. Against the company's own forward estimates the multiple compresses as EPS is expected to rise from $1.52 in FY25 to $1.83 in FY26E and $2.17 in FY27E. The dividend yield of 4.35% and the FCF yield of 3.2% frame the cash return. The consensus target of $57.52 implies the market will pay for the FY26E revenue step-up to about $6.1B; the current $46.01, near the 52-week low of $42.20, prices in more doubt.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Fee-Bearing Capital and AUM keep compounding across the five platforms, led by $326B of credit and $114B of infrastructure Fee-Bearing Capital as of June 30, 2026; fundraising stays strong, an easing rate path lifts asset values, and the multiple re-rates back toward the 52-week high of $62.57 and the top of the analyst range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue advances toward the consensus FY26E figure of about $6.1B and EPS toward $1.83, fee earnings scale steadily, and the valuation multiple holds around today's level. The shares recover part of their decline but stay below the consensus target of $57.52.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Higher-for-longer rates and market drawdowns slow fundraising and weigh on Fee-Bearing Capital; the rich 26.6x earnings and 17.9x sales multiples compress, and the shares fall below the 52-week low of $42.20.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 45%, the Bull at 30%, and the Bear at 25%. Those weights produce a probability-weighted fair value of about $52, an expected upside near +12.9% from the $46.01 price, and a bear-case downside of about {- -17.4% -}; the resulting reward/risk is roughly 0.74x. The Bull implied price of $62 sits just under the 52-week high of $62.57, and the Base implied price of $53 sits below the consensus target of $57.52, so neither leans on heroic assumptions. The Bear implied price of $38 is set below the 52-week low of $42.20 to represent a genuine drawdown, not a formality. Our target range of $50 to $60 brackets the Base case and spans roughly +8.7% to +30.4% against the current price. The combination of double-digit expected upside but a reward/risk below 1.0x and a near-evenly-split street is what holds the call at a measured BUY rather than a stronger rating.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: BAM reports a single reportable segment; the vendor breaks out no product or geographic revenue mix, so the consolidated FY25 total of $3.9B stands in for any split. Underneath it, the company runs five investment platforms, shown here by AUM and Fee-Bearing Capital (FBC) as of June 30, 2026. Credit leads by scale at $416B of AUM and $326B of FBC. Real estate carries $280B of AUM and $104B of FBC, spanning opportunistic, secondaries, core-plus and REIT products. Infrastructure holds $262B of AUM and $114B of FBC and includes a dedicated AI infrastructure fund. Private equity holds $166B of AUM and $54B of FBC. Energy holds $144B of AUM and $74B of FBC across transition and renewable strategies. Two listed vehicles anchor the permanent-capital base: an infrastructure platform with a $29.3B market capitalization and a renewable platform with a market capitalization of over $24.4B, both as of June 30, 2026.

moatFactors.name: Scale in alternatives
moatFactors.body: Over $1 trillion of AUM across five platforms spanning infrastructure, energy, private equity, real estate and credit. That scale supports large, proprietary deals that few competitors can underwrite, which the company cites as a driver of its returns.

moatFactors.name: Permanent and perpetual capital
moatFactors.body: Products include permanent capital vehicles and perpetual strategies alongside long-term private funds, so a portion of Fee-Bearing Capital is long-dated and less prone to redemption, which stabilizes fee revenue across cycles.

moatFactors.name: Diversified fee base
moatFactors.body: Fee-Bearing Capital is spread across all five platforms rather than concentrated in one, so no single strategy dominates the fee base and a weak year in any one class is cushioned by the others.

moatFactors.name: Client and distribution reach
moatFactors.body: The client base spans institutional investors and, increasingly, private wealth, and the distribution organization that reaches them is hard for a smaller manager to replicate. Breadth of channel keeps fundraising diversified across client types and geographies, which supports fee stability when any single pool pulls back.

businessMoat.durability: The platforms shown above are presented by AUM and Fee-Bearing Capital, not as a revenue split, because the vendor breaks out no product or geographic revenue mix and the company reports one consolidated segment. The durability of the fee base rests on long-dated and perpetual capital and on a diversified set of active strategies, which should smooth fundraising cycles. The main threat to durability is external: the asset management business is sensitive to financial-market and interest-rate conditions, and the 10-K notes that price fluctuations across equity, credit, rate and FX markets can materially affect performance. On balance the moat is real but not impregnable, which is why we rate it narrow rather than wide.

points: Consensus expects FY26E revenue of about $6.1B, {+ up 54% +} from $3.9B in FY25, then $7.1B in FY27E; EPS is seen rising from $1.52 to $1.83 and $2.17.

That step-up runs well above the +12.5% year-over-year growth in Q2'26 revenue of about $1B, so the full-year jump leans on a re-acceleration or on consolidation effects the latest quarter does not yet show; we treat that gap as the main risk to the base case.
Fee-Bearing Capital totaled $326B in credit, $114B in infrastructure, $104B in real estate, $74B in energy and $54B in private equity as of June 30, 2026, a base that fee growth can compound on.
A dedicated AI infrastructure fund targets demand from hyperscalers, enterprises and governments, extending the infrastructure platform into data and compute buildout.
The private wealth channel, served by semi-liquid products such as an infrastructure income fund, opens a client pool beyond the institutional base that dominates AUM today.
An eventual easing of the Federal Funds target range, held at 3.50%-3.75% in June 2026 after late-2025 cuts, would support asset values and fundraising.

management.leadership: The pack does not name BAM's executives, so we assess the organization rather than individuals. BAM fields a deep bench of investment and asset-management professionals across a wide global office network, and draws on Brookfield's heritage as an owner and operator. The MD&A frames the guiding principle as operating with a high level of integrity and a culture of collaboration to attract and retain talent. The company also stresses alignment of interests by investing Brookfield capital alongside its clients.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation centers on returning cash rather than building assets. Capital expenditure is negligible, so the business retains little for physical investment and instead deploys capital alongside its clients in the funds it manages. The dividend is the primary use of cash, and its coverage is the open question: the payout has run ahead of free cash flow, as set out under cash flow, and the pack discloses no buybacks or total debt to weigh beside it. Cash still rose in FY25 even as total equity edged lower, consistent with a distribution funded partly from outside operating cash flow. Whether that distribution can be sustained without leaning on external funding is the central capital-allocation question.
management.governance: The pack carries no proxy statement, so board composition and independence, executive pay, insider ownership and related-party terms cannot be assessed from it; we flag that gap rather than infer. What the filings do disclose still bears on governance. Per the company description, BAM operates as a subsidiary of Brookfield Corporation, so minority Class A holders sit alongside a controlling parent. The 10-K notes that some of BAM's officers and directors are not U.S. residents and that a portion of its assets sits outside the U.S., which could make service of process and enforcement of judgments difficult for investors. A fuller governance read requires the proxy, which this pack does not include.
management.insiderOwnership: The pack includes no proxy statement, so insider and significant-shareholder ownership is not disclosed here. The only ownership-relevant fact available is the controlling-parent relationship noted under governance; the precise holdings are not in the pack.

idiosyncratic: Distribution coverage: the FY25 dividend has run ahead of both earnings and free cash flow, as detailed under cash flow; if the external funding that filled the gap becomes less available, the payout or the balance sheet could come under pressure.

Internal-control scope: per the 10-K, the results of the asset management business are consolidated into BAM but were excluded from management's evaluation of internal control over financial reporting following the 2025 Arrangement, leaving a portion of reported results outside that assessment.

Non-standard metrics: the 10-K acknowledges BAM discloses certain metrics without standardized meaning, based on its own methodologies and assumptions, which can complicate comparison with peers and across periods.

Valuation: the shares carry full trailing earnings and sales multiples, detailed under valuation, yet already sit near the 52-week low of $42.20, with analyst targets running as low as $44.00; the multiple leaves little margin if the FY26E step-up disappoints.
risks.systemic: BAM's fee base moves with financial markets and interest rates. The 10-K states that price fluctuations across equity, credit, interest-rate and foreign-exchange markets can be volatile and can substantially affect the business. The MD&A sets the backdrop: U.S. real GDP growth slowed to 1.7% in the quarter ended June 30, 2026 from 2.1% the prior quarter, inflation rose to 3.5%, and the Federal Reserve held its target range at 3.50%-3.75%. Outside the U.S., Eurozone growth stayed subdued, the ECB raised rates by 25 basis points, and China's GDP slowed to 4.3%. Equity indices rose over the quarter, with the S&P 500 up 14.9% and the MSCI World up 13.3%, which supports asset values, but a reversal would cut fee-bearing capital and fundraising. Higher-for-longer rates also raise the discount applied to the long-duration real assets at the core of BAM's platforms.

body: We rate BAM a BUY with a target range of $50 to $60. The company is a leading global alternative asset manager whose scale and asset-light fee model produced a high trailing net margin, FY25 revenue growth of 16.7% to $3.9B, and $2.1B of free cash flow. At $46.01, near the 52-week low of $42.20, the shares discount a step-up to about $6.1B of FY26E revenue that consensus still expects.

The call is measured, not emphatic. Our probability-weighted fair value is about $52, an expected upside near +12.9%, but the reward/risk is roughly 0.74x and the street is split almost evenly between Buy and Hold. Valuation multiples are full, the distribution has run ahead of free cash flow, and the asset-management unit's internal-control exclusion is an open governance item. We would add on further weakness and trim into the consensus target of $57.52.
